original_value: This paper presents millimeter wave (mmWave) measurements in an indoor environment. The high demands for the future applications in the 5G system require more capacity. In the microwave band below 6 GHz, most of the available bands are occupied; hence, the microwave band above 6 GHz and mmWave band can be used for the 5G system to cover the bandwidth required for all 5G applications. In this paper, the propagation characteristics at three different bands above 6 GHz (19, 28, and 38 GHz) are investigated in an indoor corridor environment for line of sight (LOS) and non‐LOS (NLOS) scenarios. Five different path loss models are studied for this environment, namely, close‐in (CI) free space path loss, floating‐intercept (FI), frequency attenuation (FA) path loss, alpha‐beta‐gamma (ABG), and close‐in free space reference distance with frequency weighting (CIF) models. Important statistical properties, such as power delay profile (PDP), root mean square (RMS) delay spread, and azimuth angle spread, are obtained and compared for different bands. The results for the path loss model found that the path loss exponent (PLE) and line slope values for all models are less than the free space path loss exponent of 2. The RMS delay spread for all bands is low for the LOS scenario, and only the directed path is contributed in some spatial locations. For the NLOS scenario, the angle of arrival (AOA) is extensively investigated, and the results indicated that the channel propagation for 5G using high directional antenna should be used in the beamforming technique to receive the signal and collect all multipath components from different angles in a particular mobile location.

result.paraphrase: This paper examines indoor millimeter-wave (mmWave) measurements. To meet the high capacity demands of future 5G applications, the authors note that most spectrum below 6 GHz is already occupied, making the microwave band above 6 GHz and the mmWave band suitable for providing the bandwidth needed by all 5G uses. The study investigates propagation characteristics in an indoor corridor at 19, 28, and 38 GHz under line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. Five path loss models are evaluated for this environment: close-in (CI) free space path loss, floating-intercept (FI), frequency attenuation (FA), alpha-beta-gamma (ABG), and close-in free space reference distance with frequency weighting (CIF). Key statistical measures, including power delay profile (PDP), root mean square (RMS) delay spread, and azimuth angle spread, are derived and compared across the bands. The path loss results show that the path loss exponent (PLE) and line slope values for every model are below the free-space path loss exponent of 2. RMS delay spread is low for all bands in the LOS case, where only the direct path contributes at some spatial locations. In the NLOS case, the angle of arrival (AOA) is studied in detail, and the results suggest that 5G channel propagation with high-directional antennas should use beamforming to receive the signal and gather all multipath components from different angles at a given mobile location.
